notes:
SIN AND FORGIVENESS - CHAPTER OVERVIEW
- Opening quote: "There is a crack in everything, that's how the light gets in." (Leonard Cohen)

WHAT IS SIN?
- Poem 'The Sin' by Kerry poet Brendan Kennelly: Francis Xavier Skinner commits a big sin ("an Everest of error", "a mortaller") and thinks he has wounded the God of love. He congratulates himself: he cannot impress his friends, but he can wound the God of love - "There's power for you!" He wonders whether God is bored with his insignificant sins.
- Our idea of sin is shaped by our upbringing. Skinner thinks sin in some way hurts God.
- Tony Cascarino, Irish international soccer player, in his book Full Time, honestly admits having a number of affairs while married and a child with another woman, yet he could not tell his wife the truth. 
- Lesson: when one starts a deceit, it is very difficult to break away from it.
- Graham Greene, The Heart of the Matter: "He entered the territory of lies without a passport for return."
- Our way of doing morality (happiness, growth, law, service) shapes how we see sin. Sin may be seen as:
- harming ourselves or others (happiness);
- not growing to our full potential (growth);
- breaking the laws of God and Church (law);
- not doing something good for others in need (service).
- Some feel there is no such thing as sin anymore.
- Ignatius Loyola (1491-1556), founder of the Jesuits: "What is sin? Does the word have meaning any more? I have found no agreement about the notion of sin even among those most given to their studies."

SIN IN THE HEBREW SCRIPTURES: DAVID AND BATHSHEBA
- 2 Samuel 11: King David commits adultery with Bathsheba and then has Uriah the Hittite, her husband, killed.
- In the next chapter (2 Samuel 12) the prophet Nathan condemns David for his sin.
- Psalm 51, a psalm of David: "Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin."
- Psalm 51:4: "Against you, you alone, have I sinned, and done that which is evil in your sight."
- Summary of sin in the Hebrew Scriptures:
- Sin is the breaking of the Covenant.
- Sin destroys the person and the community.
- Sin need not be the end: God can forgive all sins.

JESUS AND THE SINNER
- Parables to read: The Pharisee and the Publican (Luke 18:9-14); The Prodigal Son and The Lost Sheep (Luke 15); Jesus heals and forgives the paralysed man (Matthew 9:6); the sinful woman who kisses Jesus' feet - her many sins are forgiven, so she shows great love (Luke 7:49).
- From the Sermon on the Mount: for Jesus it is what is in the heart that counts. To sin is to harden your heart to God.
- What was radically different was how Jesus treated sinners. They seemed closer to him than the scholars and leaders. He wanted to be seen with people who had a bad name.
- Mark 2:17: he did not come to call the virtuous but sinners.
- This does not mean he condones sin: he loves the sinner. The command to love is central and applies to all.

FORGIVENESS: CONDEMN THE SIN, FORGIVE THE SINNER
- The key Christian response to moral failure is forgiveness and reconciliation. It is probably the most challenging moral teaching of all.
- "To err is human, to forgive divine."
- Forgiveness is a central gospel and kingdom value. God is full of compassion, rich in mercy and love.
- The woman caught in adultery (John 8:1-11): Jesus forgives the sinner without condoning the sin: "Go your way, and from now on do not sin again." He brings her to new life and makes the onlookers think about their own lives.
- At his death Jesus forgives the thief on the cross and asks the Father to forgive those who crucified him.
- The grace to forgive enemies is the mark of great Christians down the centuries.

JUDGEMENT
- Forgiveness does not mean sin is irrelevant or that following the law of love is easy. Many people today think that since God is so forgiving, sin does not matter much. Jesus never taught that.
- The Judgement of the Nations (Matthew 25): judgement is reserved for God, who knows the human heart completely. People are separated like a shepherd separates sheep from goats.
- The grounds: "For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me, I was naked and you gave me clothing, I was sick and you took care of me, I was in prison and you visited me." (Matthew 25:35-37)
- "Truly I tell you, just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me." (Matthew 25:40)

DARKNESS AND LIGHT (JOHN) AND PAUL
- In John's gospel the symbol of sin is darkness. People who sin are children of darkness. Sin is a power at work in us and our world.
- Christ is the Light; the light has overcome the darkness.
- Liturgy: the paschal (Easter) candle is lit in the darkness at the Easter Vigil. At Baptism a candle is lit from the Easter candle and given to parents/guardians and godparents, who are told to receive the light of Christ. Sin brings darkness, Christ brings light.
- For Paul, sin is a very human condition; we are all sinners. As sin came through one man, sin is conquered by one man. The risen Christ brings a new era of salvation, free from the power of sin.
- Eucharistic prayer: "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins."
- Forgiveness was central to Jesus' life and teaching; he died so that all might be free from sin.

THE SACRAMENT OF RECONCILIATION
- Christians celebrate God's forgiveness in the sacrament of Reconciliation (also known as Confession).
- It includes: the Word of God; confession of sins; the giving of penance; prayer of sorrow; prayer of absolution.
- The Church now more often uses a communal form of reconciliation, where people gather to show that all are sinners, that sin affects the whole community, and that all seek reconciliation with one another and with God.

FAILURE AND GROWTH
- Many find Reconciliation difficult and confession has declined, especially outside Christmas and Easter, but it can be a very joyful and healing experience.
- We fail in relationships and let people down, but out of failure can come growth, healing and a better way of being. Through failings we learn about ourselves.
- The Prodigal Son by Rembrandt: the father's hands are both masculine and feminine. Henri Nouwen wrote about how, at different times of his life, he saw himself as the wasteful younger son, the jealous elder son, or the forgiving father.

AMAZING GRACE
- Written by John Newton (1725-1807), an atheist who lived a reckless life and was captain of a slave ship.
- After surviving a storm at sea that almost killed him, he became a devout Christian. He felt deep remorse for his sins and experienced the grace of God's forgiveness.
- "Amazing Grace, how sweet the sound / That saved a wretch like me. / I once was lost, but now I'm found, / Was blind but now I see."

TEACHING OF THE CATECHISM (CCC)
- The Catechism defines sin as an offence against God.
- CCC 1850: "Sin sets itself against God's love for us and turns our hearts away from it. Like the first sin, it is disobedience, a revolt against God through the will to become 'like gods', knowing and determining good and evil. Sin is thus 'love of oneself even to contempt of God'."
- Sin also goes against reason. It begins in the human heart (CCC 1873).
- Sin wounds our nature and affects our sense of community and solidarity (CCC 1872).

ORIGINAL SIN
- Original sin: the state in which we find ourselves from birth.
- It is NOT a personal sin imposed on us by the sins of others.
- It is NOT the absurdity of existence that can never be overcome.
- It does NOT mean there is nothing we can do to change the world.
- It refers to our beginnings and explains the presence of actual sin and suffering. It makes actual sin and social sin possible.
- The Christian is called to move away from original sin to a life of grace and redemption.
- The Catechism calls it a wound in our nature (CCC 1707).

MORTAL SIN AND VENIAL SIN
- Experience shows some sins cause greater destruction than others. The Bible speaks of sins that exclude one from the kingdom and sins that do not (1 Corinthians 6:9-10; Galatians 5:19-21; Ephesians 5:5 versus James 3:2; 1 John 1:8; 5:16). From this came the classification into mortal and venial.
- CCC 1857: "Mortal sin is sin whose object is grave matter and which is also committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent."
- Three conditions must ALL be met:
- Grave matter: it must be serious. Grave matter is specified by the Ten Commandments.
- Proper/full knowledge: the person must know fully what they are doing.
- Full consent: the person must choose the evil freely.
- Example: someone who commits murder, fully aware, and not forced, commits mortal sin.
- Mortal sin destroys love in the person, destroys the goodness within us and turns us away from God.
- Turning from mortal sin needs the grace of conversion, which comes from the sacrament of Reconciliation and God's forgiveness.
- CCC 1861: "Although we can judge that an act is in itself a grave offence, we must entrust judgement of persons to the justice and mercy of God."
- Venial sin: a sin that is not mortal - often not fully intended, done without full knowledge, and not involving grave matter. It allows love to continue in the person and does not completely break the relationship with God.

THE SEVEN DEADLY (CAPITAL) SINS
- 'Capital' comes from caput, the head: they lead to other sins. They are so attractive that they require other sins to get you there.
- Aquinas called them 'capital vices', making them habits.
- There is no list in scripture. The most common list: pride, greed, lust, gluttony, envy, anger, sloth.

MODERN THOUGHT ON SIN - PERSONAL SIN
- Being moral is about who we are as much as what we do, so sin is also in the heart.
- Examples: a drug-dealer continually using others and destroying innocent lives is not just committing sins but living a sinful life; a terrorist who maims and kills for a cause is following an evil path.
- So we speak of a STATE of sin as well as committing sins.
- Fundamental option: modern writers look at the total orientation of the person rather than a list of acts. Is the person trying to be good, or continually doing evil?
- Being in a state of sin = acting continuously in an unloving way, growing away from life in the Spirit. Sin is the decision of the person.
- Greater awareness of the Bible today: sin is understood in terms of the covenant relationship with God, Jesus' care and compassion for the sinner, and God's forgiveness and compassion.
- Bernard Haring: "The starting point for any Catholic teaching on sin is that Christ has redeemed us from our sinfulness. Christ's work for us cannot be understood without sin... Christ is God's act of reconciliation with us."

SOCIAL SIN
- Sin is not simply personal. From biblical times, sin has been seen primarily as the breaking of a relationship with God and neighbour. Our sin affects us and others.
- Example: a parent who in a rage physically hurts a child - it damages the child, the whole family and the parent.
- Some sin is social and affects society as a whole:
- a bomb in a marketplace kills and maims but also shatters a community, causes more hatred, violence and fear, and affects the economy;
- people who evade taxes using offshore accounts leave less money for social services everyone needs.
- Assignment: Michael Moore's film Bowling for Columbine - the case of Kayla Rowland, aged six, shot dead by another six-year-old in her class. Moore looks at poverty, social policy, media-induced fear and the power of the National Rifle Association.

STRUCTURAL SIN AND INJUSTICE
- Structural sin (structural injustice): a specific type of social sin where society itself, or structures within society, are responsible for wrongdoing. Such structures have an inherent immoral outlook that damages people and society. Structures, companies, groups and countries can be guilty of social sin.
- Obvious example: the apartheid regime in South Africa, which denied rights, including the right to vote, to non-whites.
- Other examples listed:
- racial discrimination: apartheid; ethnic cleansing in the former Yugoslavia;
- discrimination against women under the Taliban regime in Afghanistan;
- corrupt power in countries such as Zimbabwe, denying free elections;
- policies causing poverty in Latin America while the elite get rich;
- the extermination of the Jews in Nazi Germany;
- denial of democracy in countries such as Burma;
- plundering of resources such as diamonds in poor countries for Western markets;
- AIDS drugs available in the West but virtually impossible to obtain in poorer African countries;
- abuse of workers and producers in the developing world by the rich West;
- the treatment of Travellers in twenty-first-century Ireland.
- Social sin is a helpful category because it highlights evil done by groups and institutions against the rights of individuals.

SOLIDARITY: BUILDING A CIVILISATION OF LOVE
- A civilisation of love: a society that understands we all need to support, not crush, one another.
- Pope John Paul II, Sollicitudo rei socialis (On Social Concern), 1987: sin begins with the person but can become embodied in attitudes, traditions and institutions that last long after the individual.
- SRS 37: "hidden behind certain decisions, apparently inspired only by economics or politics, are real forms of idolatry: of money, ideology, class, technology."
- To overcome structures of sin, convert people: make them see the hurt they cause. The social dimension of this conversion is the virtue of solidarity.
- SRS 33: solidarity gives people a foundation from which to attack the structures of sin and build a civilisation of love.
- Solidarity is:
- the mutual support by which members of an oppressed group strengthen one another to resist injustice;
- a commitment by members of a community to promote the common good of everyone;
- a virtue that helps us respect others, to see them not as commodities to exploit but as our neighbour; it helps overcome distrust and collaborate.
- Fairtrade: an organisation that promotes justice for workers and producers in developing countries by influencing awareness and buying patterns in Western countries (Fairtrade Mark Ireland).

STRUGGLE AGAINST STRUCTURES OF SIN
- Many believe confrontation is sometimes essential for real change. Marxism believes the structures are the problem and should be overthrown.
- John Paul II said the poor sometimes need to take responsibility, struggle against injustice and stand up for their rights - e.g. shanty dwellers in Brazil or the Philippines, an American Indian of Guatemala, the Polish Solidarity movement in the 1980s.
- Martin Luther King: "...when you are forever fighting a degenerating sense of nobodiness - then you will understand why we find it difficult to wait."
- For Martin Luther King, Gandhi and others, rebellion against injustice must itself be a just and non-sinful struggle.

MORAL FAILURE: ISLAM
- Islam sees no need for a saviour to redeem people. The way to salvation is through obedience.
- God (Allah) loves and pardons those who obey God's will, revealed in the Qur'an and the teachings of Islam. Each person is free to obey or disobey.
- Those who believe and practise the Five Pillars and follow the example of Muhammad will experience peace and be saved. Those who do not will be condemned to hell, or exclusion from God's presence.
- Muslim tradition: two angels visit the dead and question them on how they lived, but the final judgement belongs to God. The Antichrist will appear but be defeated by Jesus. On the third blast of the trumpet the dead will rise to face God's judgement; the saved cross into paradise. Those whose good deeds outnumber their evil deeds reach heaven.
- Moral failure is primarily a religious concept. The great sin is SHIRK: calling any other god the true God (similar to the first commandment of the Decalogue).
- The Judaeo-Christian sense of a covenant/personal relationship with God is not present in Islam, except in the Sufi tradition. So obedience is the primary virtue; going against God's will is the great moral failure.
- Similarities with Christianity: belief in life after death, judgement of sins, heaven and hell; a scripture; the example of the prophet; putting faith into practice. Detailed Sharia law is similar to the Catholic Church's medieval manuals for confessors.
- Differences: Christianity emphasises a loving relationship with God and reconciliation/forgiveness (formalised in the sacrament of Reconciliation); Christianity has a developing distinction between Church and State, unlike Islam's relationship with the State.
- Authority: for Islam, authority lies in the Sharia; there is no hierarchy - truth is found by going back to original sources. In Catholic Christianity authority lies in the more unified teaching of church leaders.

CHIEF RABBI JONATHAN SACKS
- In The Persistence of Faith he describes a "profound redrawing of our moral landscape" whereby "sin becomes immorality, immorality becomes deviance, deviance becomes choice, and all choice becomes legitimate." Many of all faiths agree a sense of sin no longer exists.

SUMMARY
- Views of sin are shaped by views on morality. Sin is a religious term.
- In scripture sin is the breaking of one's relationship (covenant) with God. It affects the sinner and the community. God is always ready to forgive.
- Jesus lived and died so that humanity may not be lost to sin.
- The sacrament of Reconciliation celebrates God's forgiveness.
- Mortal sin destroys the relationship with God.
- Social sin affects all of society and can be inherent in structures and institutions. Solidarity is needed to counter structures of sin.
- Islam requires obedience to the laws of Allah and practice of the faith; good deeds are rewarded with paradise.

KEY TERMS
- Forgiveness and reconciliation: the Christian response to sin - pardoning the sinner and restoring relationship with God and others.
- Original sin: the state in which we find ourselves from birth; a wound in our nature that makes actual sin possible.
- Mortal sin: grave matter + full knowledge + deliberate consent; destroys love and turns us from God.
- Venial sin: less serious sin that does not completely break the relationship with God.
- Personal sin: sin committed by an individual; also a state of sin shown by a person's fundamental option.
- Social sin: sin that affects society as a whole.
- Structural sin: wrongdoing built into the structures of society, e.g. apartheid.
- Shirk: in Islam, the great sin of calling any other god the true God.
- Solidarity: mutual support and commitment to the common good of all.

rows.prompt: What three things do the Hebrew Scriptures teach about sin?
rows.model_answer: Sin is the breaking of the Covenant with God. Sin destroys the person and the community. But sin need not be the end, because God can forgive all sins, as David's prayer in Psalm 51 shows.

rows.prompt: Explain how Jesus treated sinners, giving one example from the gospels.
rows.model_answer: Jesus was radically different: sinners seemed closer to him than the leaders, and he wanted to be seen with people who had a bad name. He forgave the sinner without condoning the sin. For example, he told the woman caught in adultery, 'Go your way, and from now on do not sin again' (John 8:1-11).

rows.prompt: Explain the symbols of darkness and light in John's gospel and in the liturgy.
rows.model_answer: In John's gospel sin is darkness and sinners are children of darkness, while Christ is the Light that has overcome the darkness. At the Easter Vigil the paschal candle is lit in the darkness. At Baptism a candle lit from the Easter candle is given to parents and godparents, who receive the light of Christ.

rows.prompt: Name the five parts of the sacrament of Reconciliation.
rows.model_answer: The Word of God, confession of sins, the giving of penance, a prayer of sorrow, and the prayer of absolution.

rows.prompt: What is original sin? Mention one thing it is not.
rows.model_answer: Original sin is the state in which we find ourselves from birth; the Catechism calls it a wound in our nature. It explains the presence of actual sin and suffering. It is not a personal sin imposed on us by others, and it does not mean we can do nothing to change the world.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between mortal sin and venial sin.
rows.model_answer: A mortal sin needs grave matter, full knowledge and deliberate consent; it destroys love in the person and turns them away from God. A venial sin is less serious: it may not be fully intended or fully known and does not involve grave matter. It allows love to continue and does not completely break the relationship with God.

rows.prompt: What is social sin? Give one example.
rows.model_answer: Social sin is sin that affects society as a whole, not just individuals. For example, a bomb in a marketplace kills people but also shatters a community and causes more hatred, violence and fear. Tax evasion through offshore accounts leaves less money for social services everyone needs.

rows.prompt: What is solidarity and why did John Paul II see it as important?
rows.model_answer: Solidarity is mutual support among the oppressed, a commitment to the common good of everyone, and a virtue that helps us see others as our neighbour, not as commodities. John Paul II said it gives people a foundation to attack the structures of sin and build a civilisation of love (SRS 33).

rows.prompt: Outline the Islamic view of moral failure.

Those who practise the Five Pillars and follow Muhammad will be saved, and those whose good deeds outnumber their evil deeds reach paradise. The great sin is shirk, calling any other god the true God.

rows.prompt: Outline the Catholic Church's teaching on mortal sin and venial sin. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: The Catholic Church teaches that some sins cause greater destruction than others. The Bible speaks of sins that exclude one from the kingdom and sins that do not (e.g. 1 Corinthians 6:9-10 compared with James 3:2), and from this came the classification of mortal and venial sin. The Catechism defines mortal sin as 'sin whose object is grave matter and which is also committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent' (CCC 1857). All three conditions must be met. Grave matter means the act is serious, as specified by the Ten Commandments. Full knowledge means the person knows fully what they are doing. Full consent means they choose the evil freely. For example, a person who commits murder, fully aware and not forced, commits a mortal sin. Mortal sin destroys love in the person and the goodness within us, and turns us away from God. To turn away from it needs the grace of conversion, which comes through the sacrament of Reconciliation and God's forgiveness. Yet the Church follows Jesus, who condemned the sin but forgave the sinner: 'we must entrust judgement of persons to the justice and mercy of God' (CCC 1861). A venial sin is any sin that is not mortal. It is often not fully intended, done without full knowledge, or not grave matter. It allows love to continue in the person and does not completely break the relationship with God.

rows.prompt: 'Sin is not simply a personal matter.' Discuss this statement with reference to social sin and structural sin. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: From biblical times sin has been seen as the breaking of a relationship with God and neighbour, so our sin affects us and others. Even a personal sin, like a parent hurting a child in a rage, damages the child, the family and the parent. Some sin is social because it affects society as a whole. A bomb in a marketplace kills and maims but also shatters a community, causes hatred, violence and fear, and harms the economy. People who evade taxes through offshore accounts leave less money for social services everyone needs. Structural sin is a specific type of social sin, where society or structures within it are responsible for wrongdoing because of an inherent immoral outlook. The obvious example is apartheid in South Africa, which denied non-whites rights including the vote. Other examples are the extermination of the Jews in Nazi Germany, discrimination against women under the Taliban, plundering diamonds from poor countries for Western markets, and the treatment of Travellers in Ireland. Pope John Paul II, in Sollicitudo rei socialis (1987), said sin begins with the person but becomes embodied in attitudes, traditions and institutions that outlast the individual; behind some economic decisions lie 'real forms of idolatry: of money, ideology, class, technology'. His answer is solidarity, a commitment to the common good that helps us 'attack the structures of sin and build a civilisation of love'. Social sin is useful because it highlights evil done by groups against individuals' rights.

Must cover both social and structural sin for top marks.

rows.prompt: Discuss the importance of forgiveness in the life and teaching of Jesus, referring to at least two gospel passages. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Forgiveness and reconciliation are the key Christian response to moral failure; it is probably the most challenging moral teaching of all. What was radically different about Jesus was the way he treated sinners. They seemed closer to him than the scholars and leaders, and he was happy to be seen with people who had a bad name. He said he did not come to call the virtuous but sinners (Mark 2:17). This does not mean he condoned sin; he loved the sinner. In the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 8:1-11), Jesus forgives her without condoning the sin: 'Go your way, and from now on do not sin again.' He brings her to new life and makes the onlookers think about their own lives. In Luke 7:49 the sinful woman who kisses his feet has her many sins forgiven, and so she shows great love. Parables such as the Prodigal Son (Luke 15) show a father who welcomes his wasteful son home. Even at his death Jesus forgives the thief on the cross and asks the Father to forgive those who crucified him. Forgiveness does not mean sin does not matter: in the Judgement of the Nations (Matthew 25) people are judged on how they treated 'the least of these'. Jesus died so that all might be free from sin, as Christians remember at the Eucharist: 'my blood... poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins'.

rows.prompt: Compare the Christian and Islamic understandings of moral failure. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: In Islam salvation comes through obedience to God's will revealed in the Qur'an; there is no need for a saviour. The great sin is shirk, calling any other god the true God. Obedience is the main virtue, and there is no sense of a covenant or personal relationship with God except in the Sufi tradition. In Christianity, sin is the breaking of a loving relationship with God, and Christ redeems people from sin. Both believe in life after death, judgement of sins, and heaven and hell; both have a scripture and a prophet's example, and stress putting faith into practice. A key difference is Christianity's emphasis on reconciliation and forgiveness, formalised in the sacrament of Reconciliation. Authority also differs: for Islam it lies in the Sharia with no hierarchy, while Catholic authority lies in the teaching of Church leaders.
